clip.title: The Unsung Heroines of D-Day
clip.dialogue:
29-year-old Welsh {{blank}} Iris Bower
was one of the first British women to arrive in Normandy
after the D-Day landings in {{blank}} 1944.
She faced down hostility before she'd even reached the beaches.
"We don't want any {{blank}} women in this outfit,"
one of the medical orderlies told her.
But with the biggest amphibious {{blank}} in history under way,
women like Iris were vital to Allied victory.
Operation {{blank}}, the Allied campaign to liberate Europe
and defeat the Nazis, has long been immortalised
in Hollywood {{blank}} like Saving Private Ryan.
By August 1944, over two million soldiers
had landed in northern France to {{blank}} the Germans.
Their story is well known.
Much less well {{blank}} is the crucial role
hundreds of thousands of young women from all walks of life
played in this epic {{blank}} mission.
Undeterred by male detractors, Iris was one of two women
from the Princess Mary's Royal Air Force {{blank}} Service
who crossed the Channel five days after the invasion began.
Provisions were basic, {{blank}} in slit trenches,
washing from a bucket, bombs exploding overhead.
The nursing {{blank}} worked tirelessly
in a temporary field hospital,
where over 1,000 wounded {{blank}} were treated in under a week.
Broken, burnt, bullet-ridden men depended on them.
Iris recalls, "Their {{blank}} looking at me because I had a tin hat on,
"battle dress, a pack on my back and a big red cross on my arm,"
and she always wore her red {{blank}}.
Back in Britain, 18-year-old Ruth Bourne
was fighting the same war as {{blank}} and the men on the beaches
but from a north London outstation,
{{blank}} of the Bletchley Park code-breaking nexus.
Ruth operated the giant, noisy bombe machines
used to crack the {{blank}} Enigma codes.
In June 1944, her workload was particularly heavy.
Thousands of {{blank}} had been recruited
to intercept, translate and process these encrypted enemy messages,
{{blank}} crucial intelligence for the army fighting across France.
But no-one could know about their important work.
These women {{blank}} the Official Secrets Act,
and Ruth explains, "Once we were in, we couldn't leave.
"The stakes were {{blank}}."
Other women found themselves far nearer the action.
Much of Anti-Aircraft {{blank}},
which protected Britain against airborne attack,
had been {{blank}} by women since 1941.
They operated radar, height finders and predictors,
cutting-edge technology used to plot the course of enemy {{blank}}.
Although frequently exposed to enemy raids, their non-combatant status
{{blank}} they could do everything but load and fire the guns.
26-year-old Ena Collymore-Woodstock was one of approximately 100 women
recruited from the {{blank}}
to serve in the Auxiliary Territorial Service in Britain.
Initially, she was {{blank}} the role of clerk in Guildford, Surrey,
but Ena had not travelled all the way from Jamaica
to sit behind a {{blank}}.
"No, sir! I was tested and told I could go into any unit.
"I selected {{blank}}-aircraft and became a radar operator."
"Gunner Girl" Ena was one of thousands of ATS volunteers
posted across the Channel
to defend newly liberated north-west Europe.
In the months following D-Day,
with the Allies pushing through France and beyond,
thousands more women were required on the Continent
as cooks, orderlies, clerks, drivers and operatives.
Many young women longed to go,
although some faced strong opposition.
As Prime Minister Winston Churchill commented,
"papas and mamas" did not want their daughters serving in Europe,
heavily outnumbered by men.
Women in the military were expected to manage
sometimes overwhelming male attention and not get pregnant.
But despite the rigid gender divides and inequalities,
most women relished being part of the war effort.
It changed their lives, and they changed the outcome of the war.
Nurse Iris Bower was awarded an MBE for her war work.
Late in life, she still remembered the soldiers in her care.
"One shouted out, 'Adolf, you've had it now,' when he saw me."
Operation Overlord could not have been executed
without the dedication and work
of hundreds of thousands of brave women at home and abroad.
80 years on, their vital role in this extraordinary story
is finally getting the recognition it deserves.

slides.title: Language focus: Past Perfect

words.example: By August 1944, over two million soldiers had landed in northern France to fight the Germans.
words.translation: arrived and were already in place before the next event

words.example: Thousands of women had been recruited to intercept, translate and process these encrypted enemy messages.
words.translation: were already enlisted before the action being described

words.example: Ena had not travelled all the way from Jamaica to sit behind a desk.
words.translation: used to contrast an expectation with reality in the past

words.example: Much of Anti-Aircraft Command, which protected Britain against airborne attack, had been manned by women since 1941.
words.translation: was already staffed and operating before the period mentioned

slides.content:
The past perfect describes an action that was completed before another past event. It helps us establish a clear timeline when two things happened at different points in the past.
• Form: had + past participle (e.g. 'had landed', 'had been recruited', 'had travelled').
• Meaning: shows that one past action was already finished when a second past action occurred.
• Use: common in narratives, news reports, and documentaries to set the background before the main story moment.
In this clip, the past perfect keeps the timeline of the war crystal clear — what was already in place before D-Day even began.
